title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
Scammers deployed AI to fabricate a news article and interview featuring real public figures, including a Reserve Bank governor and an ABC finance presenter, promoting an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fake content was designed to appear credible and circulate online to deceive potential investors. This represents a model failure in which AI systems generated false statements presented as fact, combined with a deployment failure in which the fabricated content reached the public without verification of its authenticity.

The system was used outside the conditions it should have been deployed for: generating realistic-looking misinformation for financial fraud rather than legitimate purposes. What would have caught this was verification at multiple points, such as checking whether the figures had actually made these statements, whether the news outlet had published the article, or whether the cited platform was licensed. The sophistication of AI-generated deepfakes and false articles means that the burden of verification now falls on consumers and platforms to authenticate content before treating it as genuine.

It is not established whether specific AI platforms were knowingly misused by scammers or whether their safety systems failed to prevent this use.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake news article recently circulated online featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a fabricated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler. In this fictional scenario, the two had a heated argument about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. The article and interview never actually occurred, representing a growing category of sophisticated investment scams that use artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and false content.

According to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, these AI-generated scams are rapidly increasing in frequency and complexity. The regulator removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Commonly impersonated figures include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, and advertisements to lure victims into providing personal information and investing money. ASIC advises consumers to verify financial licenses through official registers before investing.
